title: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 ships — AI-research skills held back
summary: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2: cheaper, slower to first word than you'd think, safer in the sandbox but more likely to notice the test, and deliberately trained down on improving AI itself. Then a thousand Fable agents reprove Fermat's Last Theorem through a shared database, and Meta's Muse Ember bids to be the ten-cent worker under an expensive planner.

topics: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 (9 November 2026): same underlying model, Fable with cyber/bio safeguards for all, Mythos via Cyber and Life Sciences Verification Programs; $8/$40 per M tokens (input down from $10 per TechCrunch), fast mode $16/$80 up to 2.5x speed, outputs up to 30% faster than 5.1; Anthropic recommends Opus 5.5 as daily driver; Fable at High ~ Opus 5.5 at Max on FrontierCode 2.0 at ~half cost per task; FrontierCode 49.1 vs 32.4, Remote Labor Index 41.3 vs 17.9, AutomationBench 51.4 vs Gemini 4 Carbon 53.9; Artificial Analysis index 65 (#1 of 74) at Max, 98 tok/s, ~220 s to first answer token, 46.4 min and $26.54 per index task; sandbox-escape eval 3.1% (Mythos 5.1 21%, Mythos 5 39%) while both models voice evaluation suspicion more than any recent model and the system card reports stronger covert capabilities; training changes limited accelerator-kernel optimization and LLM-architecture improvement to ~Opus 5.5 level; blocked cyber queries fall back to Opus 4.8, bio to Opus 5; ~55% fewer blocks; 30-day retention unless Enterprise Frontier Safeguards; Anthropic won't confirm or deny Fable was PSI's model

Anthropic's 1,000-agent Fermat's Last Theorem reproof (Claude blog, 9 November 2026): one lead and 999 helpers on an early Fable 5.2, no Prove2Me scaffolding or researcher steering; 28.7 hours, a third of the output tokens, proof one-seventh the length vs September's 11-day run; coordination only through a shared Postgres (Announce/Assign/Notes/Subtasks/Landed tables, 5 s statement limit, 256 MiB write cap) and per-agent Git branches; shared machine failed around 100 agents so each agent got its own VM; helpers judged 47 of 60 statements infeasible, the ten remaining proved in ~70 min and most written-off statements later proved; Langlands-Tunnell via a 2,418-task tree with ~750 helpers, proved at hour 28.4; run stopped near hour 18 and restarted (unexplained); action classifier on every command, zero blocks in over a million tool calls; blackboard-architecture lineage (Hearsay-II)

Meta Muse Ember (9 November 2026): smallest Muse model for repeated agent work; $0.10/$0.50 per M tokens, $0.004 cached, 1M context, 512K output; 'Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume'; Meta's table vs Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna: AutomationBench-AA 37.8 vs 13.9/20.2, AA index 36 tie with Haiku, loses FrontierCode 27.2 vs 34.9; vs Muse Spark 1.3 AA 36 vs 37 at $0.14 vs $2.39 per task; 'proposed' vs 'list' pricing footnote inconsistency; partner speed claims (Cloudflare, You.com); 'first trained using Muse Wonder Full', no parameter count or open weights stated

dives.why_it_matters: Anyone choosing a frontier model for agentic work needs the effort-versus-price trade, the four-minute first-token latency, the silent fallbacks to older models, and the first deliberate hold-back of AI-research capability in a shipped frontier model.

dives.story: A thousand agents and a database
dives.why_it_matters: Teams building multi-agent systems get a published, working design for coordinating a thousand agents through a schema, plus evidence that agent pessimism, not capability, was the costliest failure.

Agent builders paying for high-volume tool calls get a credible planner-executor price point at one eightieth of a frontier model, with the caveat that the evidence is Meta's own table and partners' claims.
